mappings.note: Defines bryophytes by their partly differentiated body -- rhizoids, leaf-like structures, no vascular tissue -- and then explains the amphibian label from that. Body organisation, so the C4.2 competency that the whole plant-division family shares.

Spirogyra placed in Thallophyta on an undifferentiated thallus (C4.2), with a labelled drawing demanded outright, which is LO-27's 'Represent findings in multiple modes, including appropriate figures'. LO-27 is cited only where drawing is an explicit marked instruction, not wherever a figure happens to appear.

WEAK FIT, same gap as the short gymnosperm/angiosperm seed item: the comparison asked for is seed structure and reproductive features, and curriculum 82 has no plant-reproduction outcome. C4.5 was rejected because the stem asks for a contrast, not for an adaptive advantage.

Height separating leaves from roots and therefore requiring conducting tissue -- the tissue level serving the whole organism, C4.2. The long-form twin of the two-mark transport-tissue item and mapped identically; no outcome exists that would separate them.

Both halves are asked: the defining features that mark out Arthropoda (jointed appendages, segmentation -- LO-5's placement work) and how the exoskeleton lets the group survive across diverse environments (C4.5). The survival clause is why C4.5 leads.

Defines binomial nomenclature and states two of its rules -- both halves of LO-3, which fuses significance and rules into one row. Not C-4.1-LO-4: no organism of the students' surroundings is actually named.

Hydra's tissue level set against the cellular level of sponges is LO-6 word for word; the explicit 'draw a longitudinal section' instruction adds LO-27. Not C4.2-LO-5: Cnidaria has its own row and this is exactly the contrast it names.

Bilateral symmetry defined and then used to explain directed movement in flatworms -- body organisation used to characterise a phylum, LO-5. Platyhelminthes has no outcome of its own, so this sits with the other general phylum items.

The item's point is that a shared function, flight, is not a valid classification characteristic (C-4.1-LO-1 -- which characteristics may be used) and that true relationship is a matter of descent (C4.5). A rare item where rejecting a criterion is the whole task.
POOR FIT: the seven ranks explained in sequence, the fullest of the hierarchy items, and curriculum 82 has no rank-hierarchy outcome for this chapter. Cited on 'classify organisms in groups' alone.

Identify the phylum from a segmented body with a true cavity, then explain the locomotor advantage of repeating segments -- LO-7 covers both, since it names segmentation in Annelida and what such a body makes possible.

Notochord defined and then traced from protochordates, where it persists, to vertebrates, where it is replaced -- body organisation used to place animals among the chordates, LO-5. No chordate row exists to prefer.

Same counterfactual as the short one-kingdom item (LO-9, the cellular criterion behind the kingdom split), but this version asks specifically what it would do to our grasp of EVOLUTIONARY RELATIONSHIPS, which is what adds C4.5 and keeps the two items apart.

Why the reproductive innovations of angiosperms made them the most diverse group -- adaptive structure and function, C4.5. Not C4.2: the answer mentions vascular tissue in passing, but the question is about reproductive success, which has no outcome of its own.

POOR FIT on the content code -- another rank-hierarchy item, worked through a tiger, with no outcome in this curriculum covering ranks -- but the drawing instruction is explicit, so LO-27 is genuinely earned here even though C-4.1-LO-2 is a stand-in.

Fossils as the only direct physical evidence of past life and of its increasing complexity -- C4.5's 'evidences of biological evolution'. The long-form partner of the short fossil item, on the same row because C4.5 carries no outcomes to split them between.

Explains the three-domain system AND that it inserts a rank above kingdom, so it engages the succession of kingdom systems (LO-9) as well as the current understanding (C7.1). The two-mark Woese item is C7.1 alone, because it asks only who and on what basis.

Two named human threats, deforestation and pollution (C5.2, biodiversity conservation as a case study of science in human life), then the knock-on effect on dependent species (LO-15, interactions between groups of organisms). Both halves are separately marked.

A labelled starfish plus an explanation of how a calcareous endoskeleton supports an animal with no notochord -- internal body organisation, LO-5, with LO-27 for the explicit drawing instruction. Echinodermata has no outcome of its own.

Defends indigenous traditional knowledge as a contributor to classification and conservation: C6.1 for India's own contribution to the matter being studied, C5.2 for the conservation-and-ethics frame the argument is made in. Not C7.1 -- the claim is about an old knowledge system's value, not about current scientific understanding.

A laboratory procedure end to end -- collect grass, quarter-fill the bottle, add pond water, wait, mount a drop -- which is LO-25, 'Accurately use scientific instruments, apparatus and chemicals to collect data'. The only procedural item in the chapter, and no protist knowledge is actually tested, so no C4.1 code is cited.

Mangroves as physical barriers and soil microbes as chemical ones are C2.8's Earth processes and hazards; the disease barrier works through alternative hosts, which is LO-15. The long-form partner of the three-statement disaster item, mapped the same way for the same reasons.

Three parts, three rows: the flowchart drawing (LO-27), Whittaker's criteria applied to place organisms in five kingdoms (C-4.1-LO-2), and why fungi were moved out of Plantae, which is a revision of the kingdom scheme (C4.2-LO-9). Three codes is the cap and each earns its place.

Part (a) is the succession Aristotle to Linnaeus to Whittaker (LO-9); parts (b) and (c) are what binomial nomenclature is and why it was needed, which is LO-3's rules-and-significance row. No third code: (b) and (c) are two halves of one outcome, not two.

Part (a) defines endemism and hotspots and part (b) argues the threat from human activity and climate change with Indian examples -- C5.2 for the conservation case, C2.8 for the climate and habitat mechanism behind it. The rare biodiversity item where both halves of that split are demanded.
